clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive deficiency of cystathionine gamma-lyase (cystathionase), the enzyme that cleaves cystathionine to cysteine in the transsulfuration pathway
Characterised biochemically by raised cystathionine in plasma and urine
It is regarded as a benign trait with no consistent disease association, often discovered incidentally
Many cases are pyridoxine (vitamin B6) responsive, since the enzyme uses a B6-derived cofactor
Apparent clinical associations reported historically are generally attributed to ascertainment bias rather than a causal link
Secondary cystathioninuria is commoner than the primary trait and occurs in vitamin B6 deficiency, liver disease, thyrotoxicosis and neuroblastoma
The main practical task is to recognise it as benign and avoid unnecessary investigation or treatment
It must be distinguished from classical homocystinuria, in which cystathionine is low rather than high
reference.pathophysiology: In the transsulfuration pathway, homocysteine is condensed with serine to form cystathionine, which cystathionine gamma-lyase then cleaves to cysteine and alpha-ketobutyrate. When this enzyme is deficient, cystathionine accumulates and spills into the urine, producing cystathioninuria, while the downstream synthesis of cysteine is reduced but usually compensated by dietary intake. Because the enzyme is pyridoxal phosphate dependent, activity is often improved by pyridoxine. The accumulated cystathionine appears to be metabolically inert and non-toxic, which is why the primary deficiency is a benign biochemical trait rather than a disease.
additionalDifferentials: Classical homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency), where cystathionine is low
Secondary cystathioninuria from vitamin B6 deficiency
Cystathioninuria in neuroblastoma and other tumours
Other transsulfuration and remethylation pathway disorders
additionalInvestigations: Plasma and urine amino acids demonstrating raised cystathionine
Plasma total homocysteine to exclude homocystinuria
Liver and thyroid function tests to exclude secondary causes
A trial of pyridoxine to assess responsiveness
CTH gene sequencing where confirmation of the primary trait is desired
redFlags: Raised homocysteine accompanying the cystathionine, which points away from a benign trait
Clinical or biochemical evidence of an underlying tumour such as neuroblastoma
Signs of liver disease or thyrotoxicosis suggesting a secondary cause
Symptoms attributed to cystathioninuria itself, prompting reassessment
reference.prognosis: The primary trait is benign with a normal outlook and no need for long-term treatment; when cystathioninuria is secondary, prognosis is that of the underlying condition.
pitfalls: Treating a benign trait as a significant disease and overinvestigating the patient
Failing to distinguish primary cystathioninuria from important secondary causes such as neuroblastoma
Confusing it with classical homocystinuria without measuring homocysteine
Overlooking simple pyridoxine responsiveness when documenting the biochemistry
references: Mudd SH et al. Transsulfuration pathway disorders review
